name: Confucius
info: Confucius (c. 551 – c. 479 BCE), born Kong Qiu, was a Chinese philosopher and teacher of the Spring and Autumn period in the state of Lu, whose teachings on morality, family and government became Confucianism.

facts.born: Thought to have been born on 28 September 551 BCE in Zou (in modern Qufu, Shandong), in the state of Lu; son of Kong He, commandant of the local Lu garrison, of the shi class
facts.died: c. 479 BCE in Lu, of natural causes, at the age of 71 or 72; buried on the bank of the Sishui River, north of Qufu
facts.role: Teacher from after the age of 30; governor of a town in Lu (from 501 BCE), then Minister of Crime; left Lu in 497 BCE; adviser to officials of Lu after his return at 68
facts.known: The teachings called Confucianism; the Analects, compiled by his followers; the Silver Rule; filial piety and rule by virtue rather than punishment; teaching students of every class; the Five Classics, by traditional attribution

t: Born into the shi class of Lu and raised in poverty, Confucius began teaching after he turned 30 and accepted students whatever their background.
As an official of Lu he tried to restore the duke's authority by having the three great families raze their walled strongholds, failed at the last of them and left the state in 497 BCE.
His teaching that government should rest on virtue and ritual rather than law and punishment became the official philosophy of imperial China under Emperor Wu of Han.
dyk: Confucius asked no tuition of a prospective student, only a symbolic gift of a bundle of dried meat. The name Confucius itself was coined in the late 16th century by early Jesuit missionaries to China, as a Latinized form of Kongfuzi.
ev: Kong Qiu is thought to have been born at Zou, in the state of Lu
Yang Hu, a retainer of the Ji family, rebels and seizes power in Lu
After Yang Hu is expelled, Confucius is appointed governor of a town, later rising to Minister of Crime
Hou Fan's revolt at Hou opens the way for Confucius to press the three families to dismantle their strongholds
The walls of Hou and Bi are razed, but Duke Ding's siege of Cheng fails
Confucius leaves Lu and begins years of travel among the states of north-east and central China
He dies in Lu at the age of 71 or 72 and is buried north of Qufu

sections.early:
Confucius was born Kong Qiu; it is thought that he was born on 28 September 551 BCE in Zou, in modern Qufu, Shandong. The area was in law controlled by the kings of Zhou but was effectively independent under the local lords of Lu, who ruled from the nearby city of Qufu. His father, Kong He (or Shuliang He), was an elderly commandant of the local Lu garrison. Traditional accounts trace the family through the dukes of Song to the Shang dynasty and relate that Kong He's grandfather had moved the family from Song to Lu; not all modern scholars accept this descent from Song nobility.

Kong He died when Confucius was three years old, and his mother, Yan Zhengzai, raised him in poverty; she died at less than 40 years of age. He was born into the class of shi, between the aristocracy and the common people, and was educated at schools for commoners, where he learned the Six Arts. At 19 he married Qi Guanshi; a year later they had a son, Kong Li, and later two daughters. He is said to have worked in various government jobs in his early twenties, and as a bookkeeper and a caretaker of sheep and horses, and to have mourned his mother for three years, as was the tradition.

His courtesy name, given at his coming of age, was Zhongni. The name Confucius is a Latinized form of Kongfuzi, roughly "Great Master Kong", coined in the late 16th century by early Jesuit missionaries to China; the more common Mandarin name today is Kongzi, "Master Kong". His lifetime saw a rich diversity of thought and was a formative period in China's intellectual history.
sections.rise:
Confucius began teaching after he turned 30. He pioneered private education in China, with a curriculum known as the Six Arts, and he considered his students' background irrelevant: he accepted noblemen, commoners and even former criminals, charged no tuition and asked a prospective student only for a symbolic gift of a bundle of dried meat, while disciples from richer families paid a sum in keeping with their wealth. Most of his recorded disciples came from Lu, but others came from Wey, Qin, Chen, Qi, Cai, Chu and Song.

In his time Lu was headed by a ducal house, under which three aristocratic families, the Ji, the Meng and the Shu, held hereditary offices. In the winter of 505 BCE Yang Hu, a retainer of the Ji family, rebelled and seized power from it, and by the summer of 501 BCE the three families had expelled him from Lu. By then Confucius had built up a considerable reputation through his teaching, and the families had come to see the value of proper conduct and righteousness in securing loyalty to a legitimate government.

In that year, 501 BCE, Confucius was appointed to the minor position of governor of a town, and he eventually rose to be Minister of Crime. It was likely as a consequence of Yang Hu's failed coup that his first disciples were appointed to government positions, some of them arranged by Confucius himself; Zhong You was made a governor by the Ji family by his arrangement. The Ji family gave his disciples many opportunities for employment even though Confucius disapproved of its practices and was openly critical of it.
sections.deeds:
In office Confucius sought to return the authority of the state to the duke by dismantling the fortified strongholds of the three families. After a revolt at Hou in 500 BCE against the Shu family, he and his disciples spent a year and a half persuading the families to raze the walls of Hou, Bi and Cheng. Gongshan Furao, a retainer of the Ji family, then revolted at Bi and entered the capital; Confucius ordered two officers to attack the rebels, who were pursued and defeated at Gu, after which the Ji family razed the walls of Bi.

His lasting work was his teaching. In the Analects, compiled many years after his death, he presents himself as a "transmitter who invented nothing" and puts the greatest emphasis on study. He taught self-cultivation, the emulation of moral exemplars and skilled judgment rather than knowledge of rules, and his ethics rest on three linked ideas: li, the rites, institutions and etiquette of daily behaviour; yi, righteousness, doing the right thing for its own sake; and ren, often translated as benevolence or humaneness. One teaching, sometimes called the Silver Rule, reads: "Never impose on others what you would not choose for yourself."

His political thought rested on his ethics. He argued that the best government rules through rites and morality rather than incentives and coercion: people led by laws and punishments avoid the punishment but have no sense of shame, while those led by virtue become good. He looked back to earlier ages for a unified royal state whose rulers would succeed by moral merit instead of lineage.
sections.opponents:
The Xunzi says that on becoming Minister of Crime Confucius ordered the execution of Shaozheng Mao, another official and scholar of Lu, on a charge of "five crimes" that included "concealed evilness" and "eloquent duplicity". His programme in Lu failed at its last step: the governor of Cheng persuaded the head of the Meng family not to raze its walls, arguing, as the Zuo Zhuan recalls, that this would leave Cheng open to the state of Qi, and when Duke Ding of Lu besieged Cheng in 498 BCE he did not succeed. Confucius had made powerful enemies in the state.

At the courts of the states he visited afterwards he expounded his political beliefs but did not see them put into practice. Towards the end of the Warring States period Legalism, considered an "antithesis of Confucian thinking", held that humanity and righteousness were not sufficient in government and that rulers should rely on statecraft, punishments, the vigorous administration of law and warfare; the Qin state, which conquered all of China in 221 BCE, adopted it as its official doctrine.

In the early 20th century intellectuals and activists condemned Confucianism as a cause of the Qing dynasty's close-mindedness and refusal to modernize. During the Cultural Revolution the Chinese Communist Party held that Confucius and Confucianism represented reactionary ideologies of the slave-owning aristocracy; Red Guards attacked his tomb, and from 1973 to 1976 Mao Zedong's Criticize Lin, Criticize Confucius campaign presented him as a defender of a slave state and the charges against Shaozheng Mao as trumped-up.
sections.last:
According to the Zuo Zhuan and the Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), Confucius left Lu in 497 BCE after the failure of the attempt to dismantle the walls of the three families. The Shiji tells that the neighbouring state of Qi, worried that Lu was growing too powerful, sent the duke of Lu 100 good horses and 80 dancing girls, and that the duke neglected his duties for three days. In this account Confucius waited for a lesser fault so as not to shame his ruler in public, and left when the duke failed to send him his due portion of sacrificial meat.

He travelled through the states of north-east and central China, among them Wey, Song, Zheng, Cao, Chu, Qi, Chen and Cai. According to the Zuo Zhuan he returned to Lu when he was 68, invited by Ji Kangzi, the chief minister. The Shiji depicts him spending his last years teaching 3,000 pupils, of whom 72 or 77 mastered the Six Arts, and writing or editing the Five Classics, a traditional attribution that modern scholars treat with caution. He sometimes advised officials of Lu, Ji Kangzi among them, on governance and crime.

Burdened by the loss of his son and of his favourite disciples, he died of natural causes at the age of 71 or 72, in about 479 BCE, and was buried on the bank of the Sishui River, north of Qufu. His disciples and his only grandson, Zisi, continued his school after his death. The humble tomb was enlarged by emperors from the Han dynasty onwards; the Cemetery of Confucius now covers 183 hectares, holds more than 100,000 graves of his Kong descendants and is on the World Heritage List.
sections.legacy:
His disciples and followers organized his teachings into the Analects. Mencius, in the 4th century BCE, stressed the innate goodness of human beings, and Xunzi, in the 3rd, the shaping of morality by tradition and training. After a setback under the Qin, the works attributed to Confucius were made the official imperial philosophy under Emperor Wu of Han and, in 140 BCE, required reading for the civil service examinations, which continued nearly unbroken until the end of imperial China in 1912. In the Song dynasty the teaching was revived as what is now called Neo-Confucianism, whose most renowned scholar was Zhu Xi; it held sway in China, Japan, Korea and Vietnam until the 19th century.

Jesuit missionaries first translated the works into European languages in the 16th century; a team of them published several in Paris in 1687, and such works are thought to have mattered to Deists and other thinkers of the Enlightenment. His descendants were honoured with titles: that of Duke Yansheng, first bestowed in 1055, lasted until the Nationalist government abolished it in 1935. The Kong family tree, now in its 83rd generation, has two million known and registered descendants.

Some follow Confucianism in a religious manner, while many argue that it is less a religion than a secular morality. After the attacks of the Maoist era, veneration resumed in the early 1980s with Communist officials in attendance; in Taiwan the memorial ceremony continued without interruption. Modern scholars are cautious about attributing specific assertions to Confucius himself.

summary: Confucius (c. 551 – c. 479 BCE), born Kong Qiu in the state of Lu, taught students of every class and served Lu as an official before leaving it in 497 BCE. His teachings on virtue, ritual and government, gathered in the Analects after his death, became the official philosophy of imperial China from the Han dynasty.

H. G. Creel, Confucius: The Man and the Myth (John Day Company, 1949)
Daniel K. Gardner, Confucianism: a very short introduction (Oxford Univ. Press, 2014)
Michael Hunter, Confucius Beyond the Analects (BRILL, 2017)
Yong Huang, Confucius: A Guide for the Perplexed (A&C Black, 2013)

Birth: lead 'c. 551', text 'it is thought ... 28 September 551 BCE': circa true. Death: lead 'c. 479 BCE' only; no day or place of death is stated (place 'in Lu' inferred from the return home and burial at Qufu): editor may cut 'in Lu' from facts.died and the last event.
Age at death '71 or 72' as the article gives it. The year of his return to Lu is not given (only 'when he was 68'), so it is not an event.
The article gives two accounts of the departure from Lu (Zuo Zhuan/Shiji: after the failed dismantling, 497 BCE; Shiji: the gift of horses and dancing girls); both are given, attributed.

Execution of Shaozheng Mao is attributed to the Xunzi only, as in the article. The article's clause on his lectures drawing 'the three thousand disciples several times except Yan Hui' is garbled and was left out.
Creel's and Dubs's differing views of Gongshan Furao's revolt were left out for length.
The 140 BCE date for the examinations' required reading is as the article states it.
'Never impose on others...' is the article's translation of Analects 15.24 (the article does not give the passage number).
